title: Marriage (Mark 10:1–12)
hookLine: asked about divorce, he points back to creation; churches today apply this in differing ways

cards: Chapter ten, and the road turns south. Jesus leaves Galilee for Judea and the land beyond the Jordan, and crowds gather again. Some Pharisees come with a question, and Mark tells us it's a test.

Is it lawful for a man to put away his wife? The Law of Moses allowed a man to write his wife a certificate of divorce and send her away, and teachers disagreed sharply over what reasons were good enough.
Whatever Jesus says, someone will be unhappy. Almost everyone listening knows a marriage that held, and one that broke. He goes not to the rules, but back to the beginning.

teach.b: What did Moses command, he asks. Moses allowed a certificate of divorce, they say.

teach.h: FOR THE HARDNESS OF YOUR HEART.
teach.b: Jesus says Moses wrote that because of the hardness of your hearts. It's a different Greek word from the hard hearts in the boat on day one ninety-one, but the same picture: a heart gone stiff.
Then he reaches past Moses to Genesis: from the beginning God made them male and female, and a man shall leave his father and mother, and the two shall be one flesh.
Then the line still heard at weddings, in the King James Bible: "What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder." Asunder means apart.

Later, in the house, he goes further with the disciples: whoever divorces and marries another commits adultery. Mark also includes a wife divorcing her husband, which fit Roman law more than the Jewish custom of the day.
And divorce then often meant a woman sent away with a piece of paper, and often nothing to live on. Many readers hear in his words a protection for the one most likely to be discarded.

Churches apply this differently, and each takes it seriously. The Catholic Church teaches that a valid sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved, and it can declare that a marriage was never valid, an annulment.
Orthodox churches hold marriage as lifelong, yet may allow a second marriage with a service of repentance.
Many Protestant churches allow divorce in some circumstances, such as adultery or abandonment, reading this alongside Matthew and Paul.

teach.h: WHAT THEREFORE GOD HATH JOINED TOGETHER, LET NOT MAN PUT ASUNDER.
teach.b: What they share is the starting point Jesus chose: not the loophole, but the beginning.

how: Many Christian wedding services echo Mark 10:9, that what God has joined no one should put asunder, and many churches pray for married couples during worship; churches differ on divorce and remarriage, from the Catholic Church's annulment process to the Orthodox and many Protestant churches' provisions for remarriage.

games.q: you're being tested with a hot question: is it lawful to divorce? teachers disagree about the reasons. how do you answer?
o: go back to the beginning of creation.
games.why: he asks what Moses commanded, then reaches past him to Genesis: two become one flesh. "What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder."

practice: Hold one marriage in your mind: your own, your parents', a friend's, a couple just starting, one that's struggling right now, or even one that ended, and the people still living with that.
Picture them both kindly: what do they need? Patience, time together, rest. If you pray, pray for them by name; if you don't, wish them well, slowly and on purpose.
